summary: For ages 5–7: observe and describe that there is MORE daylight in summer and LESS in winter, tying this relative pattern to the seasons and to changes in weather and nature. Stay with relative 'longer/shorter days' comparisons, not counted hours, and deliberately do NOT teach the axial-tilt cause (a later topic). Anchor in the child's lived experience across the year and keep explanations to observed daylight length, not distance from the Sun.
misconceptions: It is colder in winter because Earth is further from the Sun and warmer in summer because it is closer (the classic distance misconception — avoid seeding it here, correct it fully later).
Summer is hot only because the Sun is bigger or closer, not because days are longer.
The amount of daylight is the same all year, or day and night are always equal in length.
Seasons and shorter winter days are caused simply by clouds or 'it just gets cold'.

activities.title: A year in a slider: watch the daylight grow and shrink
steps: Drag a month handle across a year and watch a daylight bar stretch toward summer and shrink toward winter while the same garden scene shifts from a dark, short winter's day to a long, bright summer evening.

Watch a little clock show it's still dark at wake-up in winter but light at bedtime in summer, with no numbers — relative length only. (December is winter and June is summer north of the equator; it is the other way round in the Southern Hemisphere.)
Say out loud what you notice as you slide from winter toward summer: 'more daylight in summer, less daylight in winter.'
Keep sliding forward past December into the next year, and watch the bar grow and shrink again, to see that the pattern repeats every year.
activities.insight: There is more daylight in summer and less in winter, and this is a smooth, repeating yearly pattern. In most places away from the equator you can see it from your own window.

activities.title: Winter morning vs summer evening: two scenes side by side
steps: Look at a two-panel scene: a dark winter morning and a light summer evening.
Tap each panel to reveal a daylight bar and a clock face — short/dark for winter, long/light for summer.
Describe the contrast in your own words: 'In winter it's dark when I get up; in summer it's still light at bedtime.'
activities.insight: Summer has more daylight and winter has less. You can see a clue to this in the scenes: it is still dark on a winter morning, but still light on a summer evening. To make a fair comparison, look at the same time of day in each season.

activities.title: Record the change yourself over real weeks
steps: Mark on a simple chart roughly when it gets dark (soon after sunset) over several weeks, using pictures or a clock face rather than numbers. The change is easiest to see in autumn or spring.
Notice whether the dark-time is getting earlier or later and say which way it is moving.
Pair the daylight amount with seasonal cues — colder and darker in winter, warmer and lighter in summer — as patterns that go together.
Place the shortest (winter) and longest (summer) days on a year timeline or four-seasons wheel.
activities.insight: The amount of daylight really does change across the year, and it goes together with seasonal changes in weather and nature; the pattern repeats every year.

activities.title: Check and sort: season to more-or-less daylight
steps: Sort summer into 'more daylight' and winter into 'less daylight,' then place spring and autumn in between.
Put the four seasons in order so you can see the cycle repeat.
Answer: when are the days longest, and when are they shortest?
Explain how you know using something you have noticed about summer evenings and winter evenings.
activities.insight: You can reliably tell which seasons have more or less daylight and back it up with an observation, not just a memorised answer.

checkQuestion: In summer, do we get more hours of daylight or fewer than in winter? … Now tell me how you know — what have you noticed about summer evenings and winter evenings?
checkAnswer: More daylight in summer, fewer hours in winter — justified from lived observation, e.g. 'in summer it's still light when I go to bed; in winter it's dark by teatime.'
